== The first death ==
In the oldest memories of the Grey Orchard, the trees were alive. They could speak and walk and climb down from their branches and stand tall as the guardians they were. It was they who made the soil fertile and who ensured that the fruit was sweet. And it was they who guarded the people who lived among them, and kept out the beasts of the forest.
The trees were one with the land, and they knew that as the soil grew more fertile, the orchard would become more fruitful. The trees knew that, as the fruit was plucked from their branches, they would bear fruit again, in time.
And so they did, with great pleasure.

Essa fell, but the name remained in her hand. Her mother knelt beside her and called her once, then twice. There was no answer. Thus death entered the world, not as a hunter, but as the silence between two calls.

The Mother Pear felt the weight of the girl’s stillness. She searched her roots for the life she had been holding and found that she could no longer hold it. Every leaf in the orchard turned grey.

For seven nights the tree wept sap the colour of ash. The mother stayed beneath her, warming Essa’s hands between her own. On the eighth morning the Mother Pear bent until her leaves touched the woman’s hair.

“I am sorry,” she said. “I could not hold her.”

The mother looked up into the branches, where so many names still shone.

“Then let me hold her a little longer.”

So the tree lowered the broken branch beside the girl. Its white roots curled around her gently, and its leaves sheltered her from the rain. It became the first grave-tree, whose blossoms open only for those who are leaving.

The mother would not give it Essa’s name. She carried it through every season, until it softened in her palm and became the first pear. When at last she ate it, she planted the seeds beside the grave.

After that, the orchard bore fruit, and the fruit ripened and fell. Some say this was the Mother Pear’s punishment. Others say it was her promise that what she could not keep, she would help the world remember.

This is why pears taste sweetest just before they spoil, and why, at dawn, the orchard is grey.
